explain.say: In 1784 a Berlin magazine asked, what is Enlightenment? The philosopher Immanuel Kant answered: it is growing up, having the courage to use your own reason without a guardian telling you what to think. His motto, borrowed from the poet Horace, was dare to know. Look at the timeline of thinkers who tried exactly that.

explain.say: Here are the big ideas. John Locke said people have natural rights. Montesquieu said split power into three branches, lawmakers, government and judges, so no one grows too strong. Rousseau said power should come from the people, a social contract. Which of these can you see in a constitution today?

explain.say: Ideas need roads. Look at the network. Books, letters and journals linked salons in Paris, coffee houses in London, universities in Edinburgh and printers in Philadelphia. The philosopher Jürgen Habermas called this new world of debate the public sphere. Where do people argue in public today?

draw.text: Habermas: the public sphere grew in coffee houses and the press.

explain.say: Some kings borrowed these ideas. Frederick the Second of Prussia and Catherine the Great of Russia called themselves enlightened while keeping full power. And in 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft asked why reason and rights should stop at men. Why might a king like Enlightenment ideas, but only up to a point?

explain.say: Now the debate. See both sides. Some historians stress toleration, science and rights. Others, like Max Horkheimer and Theodor Adorno, warned that reason can become a tool of control, and many thinkers excluded women and enslaved people. Lovely thinking. Exam tip: Jonathan Israel splits a radical from a moderate Enlightenment; use that to show nuance.

faq.a: An intellectual movement of the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in Europe and the Americas that urged people to use reason, evidence and debate to question tradition, religion's political power and absolute rule.
asks: What did Kant mean by dare to know?

faq.q: What did Montesquieu mean by separation of powers?
faq.a: In The Spirit of the Laws, 1748, Montesquieu argued that liberty is safest when making laws, carrying them out and judging cases are held by separate bodies that check each other. The United States Constitution borrowed the idea.

faq.q: Was the Enlightenment only for some people?
faq.a: Its ideals were universal, but many thinkers excluded women, and some, such as Hume and Kant, wrote racist passages. Others, like Condorcet, argued for abolition of slavery and rights for women. Historians now study both.

A huge French reference work edited by Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert from 1751. It aimed to gather all useful knowledge and quietly criticised superstition and arbitrary power, so it was censored.
In A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792, she argued that women seem less rational only because they are denied education, and that rights based on reason must include women.

facts: Kant's essay answering What is Enlightenment? appeared in 1784.
Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws was published in 1748.
The first volume of the Encyclopédie appeared in 1751.

quiz.say: Which thinker argued that power should be split into separate branches?
quiz.show: Separation of powers is linked above all with…
quiz.why: Montesquieu argued in 1748 that lawmaking, government and judging should be held by different bodies.

wrong.1: Rousseau is known for the social contract and the general will.
wrong.2: Wollstonecraft argued for women's rights and education.

quiz.say: What did Habermas call the world of debate in coffee houses, salons and newspapers?
quiz.why: Habermas described a public sphere where private people debated public matters.

wrong.1: The general will is Rousseau's idea of the people's shared interest.
wrong.2: The longue durée is the Annales school's long-term time scale.
